title: The Nepal Flood: Trekking Impact
excerpt: The 26 August flood in Rasuwa became one of the worst disasters in Nepal's history. What happened, where things stand now, and what it means for the spring 2027 trekking season.
seoTitle: The 2026 Nepal Flood: What It Means for Trekking in Spring 2027

content.title: ✦ Updated
content.value: This article was updated with the latest casualty figures, the state of the trekking routes in Nepal, and the separate flood in the Manaslu area on 11 October.

On 26 August 2026, at about nine in the morning, a huge surge of water, mud and rock burst down the river valley in Rasuwa district in northern Nepal, near the border with Tibet. Within minutes, roads, bridges and whole villages along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers were swept away. It is one of the worst disasters in Nepal's history: according to Nepal's national disaster authority, as of 20 September more than 1,450 people had been killed and more than 5,000 were still missing, among them hundreds of foreign nationals.
Our hearts are with the families and the people of Rasuwa. In this article we sum up what happened, where things stand now, and what it means for the next trekking season in Nepal.
What happened

No rain fell in the area that day, and that is the key to understanding the disaster. A huge avalanche of ice and rock broke loose high in the mountains and blocked a small river called the Lende. Water built up behind the blockage as if behind a makeshift dam, and when it gave way the whole volume was released at once and burst downstream.

The force was extreme: downstream, the river rose by about nine meters within half an hour. Views on the initial trigger differ. One assessment links the avalanche to a minor earthquake on the Tibetan side of the border, while others believe it was a glacier collapse. The wider background is clear: the Himalaya is warming, and the risk of ice collapses like this is growing.

content.caption: Langtang Lirung; the glacier collapsed on the slopes to its north · Photo: Stefanos Nikologianis, CC BY 2.0

content.value: The damage to infrastructure is especially heavy. The Rasuwagadhi border crossing, the main crossing between Nepal and Tibet, was destroyed, with damage on the Tibetan side too. Dozens of bridges were damaged, long stretches of road were washed away, and hydropower plants along the river were hit.
Where things stand now

items: Langtang and Gosaikunda: reopened for trekking in late October, after a temporary bridge was installed at Betrawati. According to the Trekking Agencies' Association of Nepal, there are two access routes into the valley, and trail conditions are worth checking before you set out.
The Rasuwagadhi crossing into Tibet: still closed, with no official reopening date. The overland journey to Mount Kailash through it is not expected to resume in the coming season.

Manaslu: on 11 October a separate flood struck the Budhi Gandaki valley, damaging bridges and sections of trail on the way to the Manaslu Circuit and the Tsum Valley. Trekking on the Manaslu Circuit was restricted, the Tsum Valley was closed, and the Nepal Tourism Board advised postponing treks in the area until updated route information is published.
Everest and Annapurna: not affected, and the fall season there ran as usual.

content.value: What it means for the next trekking season

The next trekking season in Nepal is spring, from March to May 2027. The Everest and Annapurna regions, where most treks go, lie hundreds of kilometers from Rasuwa and the Budhi Gandaki valley, in other river systems, and the disasters did not touch them. Our own fall groups left as planned: our October group to Mera Peak, in the Everest region, reached the summit on 15 October, and our Annapurna Circuit group set out on 4 October.

In spring 2027 we run Everest Base Camp, the Annapurna Circuit and Mera Peak, and none of these departures passes through the affected areas. Anyone planning a trek in Langtang, the Tsum Valley or the Manaslu Circuit should confirm the state of trails and bridges with a local operator close to departure, because conditions there are still changing.

content.value: What HighAir is doing

We are following the situation in Nepal closely, in constant contact with our local teams and partners. The safety of our travelers comes first in every decision, and if anything changes for any of our routes, we will update registered participants directly and immediately. Our thoughts are with Nepal, with the people of Rasuwa and with every family still waiting for news.
Frequently asked questions
What caused the flood in Rasuwa?

An avalanche of ice and rock blocked a small river called the Lende high in the mountains. Water built up behind the blockage, and when it gave way it was released all at once and burst downstream. It was not a monsoon flood, and no rain fell in the area that day.
How many people were affected?
According to Nepal's national disaster authority, as of 20 September 2026, 1,451 people had been killed and 5,786 were missing, among them 636 foreign nationals. The figures are still being updated.
Are the Everest Base Camp and Annapurna treks affected?

No. The flood hit the Langtang area in Rasuwa district, north of Kathmandu, while the Everest region in the east and Annapurna in the west are hundreds of kilometers away. The fall season there ran as usual, and our spring 2027 departures do not pass through the affected areas.
Is the Langtang trek open?

Langtang and Gosaikunda reopened for trekking in late October 2026, after a temporary bridge was installed at Betrawati. Access is still limited, so check road and trail conditions close to departure.
Is the Manaslu Circuit open?

After the flood in the Budhi Gandaki valley on 11 October 2026, trekking on the Manaslu Circuit was restricted and the Tsum Valley was closed. The Nepal Tourism Board advised postponing treks in the area until further notice, so confirm the state of the route before you fix dates.
Is it safe to travel in Nepal now?

The main trekking regions, Everest and Annapurna, are operating normally and were not affected. The affected areas are recovering, and conditions there are worth checking close to departure. It is always best to travel with an operator in contact with local partners and to follow the guidance of the authorities.
